blocks.text: Although it is by no means necessary to understand the viper precisely in that place. For even though אפעה ephe properly means the viper, as what we have taught so far amply proves, it is nevertheless certain that among the Arabs the word افعي [afʿī] ephe extends much more widely. This is proved by the following words of Avicenna, Canon book 4, Fen 4, tract. 3, ch. 3, which is On the Cure of Leprosy: ولا يجب ان تكون الافعي سبخية او ريغية ولا رقية ولا شطية فانها في الاكثر قليلة المنفعة ولكثير منها غاياة التعطيش والاتلاف به [wa-lā yajibu an takūna al-afʿī sabakhiyya aw rīghiyya wa-lā raqqiyya wa-lā shaṭṭiyya fa-innahā fī al-akthar qalīlat al-manfaʿa wa-li-kathīr minhā ghāyāt al-taʿṭīsh wa-al-itlāf bihi] [col. 366] بل تختار الجبلية لاسيما البيض [bal tukhtār al-jabaliyya lā siyyamā al-bīḍ] The alephe (viper) should not be from salty places, or muddy ones, or riverbanks, or seashores; for such a one is, for the most part, of little efficacy. Above all, among these the one that excites a deadly thirst (the dipsas) is fatal. Let a mountain one therefore be chosen, especially a white one, etc. And in book 5, in the chapter On Troches made from Viper's Flesh: وليس يصلح لهذه الاقراص كل الافاعي بل شقر [wa-laysa yaṣluḥu li-hādhihi al-aqrāṣ kull al-afāʿī bal shuqr] Not all alaphai are suitable for these troches, but only the yellow ones, etc. And a little later: ويجب ان تجتنب الضارنة والرقم والرقش الضارية الي البياض ولا تصطاد من السباخ وشطوط الاودية الانهار والبحار ولا المشجرة فان فيها البلوطية الخبيثة المعطشة [wa-yajibu an tujtanaba al-ḍārina wa-al-ruqm wa-al-ruqsh al-ḍāriya ilā al-bayāḍ wa-lā tuṣṭād min al-sibākh wa-shuṭūṭ al-awdiya al-anhār wa-al-biḥār wa-lā al-mushajjara fa-inna fīhā al-ballūṭiyya al-khabītha al-muʿṭisha] And the horned ones (vipers) must be rejected, and the variegated or two-coloured ones tending toward white. Nor should they be sought from salty places, or the banks of torrents and rivers, and the shores of seas; nor from trees, because in them are the dryini, foul and thirst-exciting. And in the chapter On the Species of Serpents, which is book 4, Fen 6, tract. 3, ch. 21: والطبقة الثانية من الافاعي ونحوها ايضا مختلفة منها الافاعي الاصلية ومنها الافاعي البدوطية ومنها [III, 136] المعطشة وساير ما نذكر [wa-al-ṭabaqa al-thāniya min al-afāʿī wa-naḥwihā ayḍan mukhtalifa minhā al-afāʿī al-aṣliyya wa-minhā al-afāʿī al-badūṭiyya wa-minhā al-muʿṭisha wa-sāyir mā nadhkuru] The second order is that of the alaphai (or vipers) and similar creatures, whose species are diverse. For among them are alaphai ῥιζίαι [rhiziai], that is, those living in the roots of trees; likewise alaphai dryinae, and thirst-exciting ones, and the rest, which we shall mention. That is, according to the teaching of the Arabs there are three orders of serpents. The first contains those whose bite rejects all medicine and kills within three hours. The second, those that are treated by vomiting and by eating salted foods, and that bring death only on the third day after the bite. The third, those whose bite is not usually lethal, and is treated only by external remedies and by binding the affected part, so that the poison does not creep further. Further, since vipers are the best known in that second order of serpents, it came about that the name of vipers was common to all serpents of the same order. Therefore the Hebrew אפעה ephe, although it properly means the viper, could nevertheless, like the Arabic أفعى [afʿā], extend more widely; and hence it happens that interpreters pull this word apart into such diverse meanings. Nor were the Hebrews or the Arabs alone in so stretching the name of the viper: for in Aëtius the dipsas is defined as a species of viper that is found more in coastal places. And in Antipater of Sidon, Anthology book 3, ch. 16:
— — — — διψὰς ἔχιδνα Σαρκὶ τὸν ἐκ γενύων πικρὸν ἐνεῖσα χόλον, [— — — — dipsas echidna Sarki ton ek genyōn pikron eneisa cholon,] [col. 367]
the dipsas viper, injecting into the flesh the bitter poison from its jaws. And Nazianzen, Iamb. 22:
Διψὰς τίς ἐστι τῶν ἐχιδναίων γενῶν, [Dipsas tis esti tōn echidnaiōn genōn,]

There is a certain dipsas of the viper kind. Galen too, On Simples book 11, ch. 1, mentions vipers with the surname διψάδων [dipsadōn], by which τοὺς δηχθέντας φασὶν οὐκ ἐμπίπλασθαι πίνοντας, ἀλλὰ διαῤῥήγνυσθαι πρότερον, ἢ παύσασθαι διψῶντας [tous dēchthentas phasin ouk empiplasthai pinontas, alla diarrhēgnysthai proteron, ē pausasthai dipsōntas], they say those bitten are never sated by drinking, but burst in the middle before their thirst is allayed. It is evident that dipsades are described, which are taken for vipers because of the similarity of form. For, as Lucian asserts in the Dipsads, ἡ διψὰς ἐστιν ὄφις οὐ πάνυ μέγας, ἐχίδνῃ ὅμοιος [hē dipsas estin ophis ou pany megas, echidnē homoios], the dipsas is a serpent not very large, similar to a viper. And Nicander, Theriaca, verse 266:
Ναὶ μὴν δίψαδος εἶδος ὁμώσεται αἰὲν ἐχίδνῃ, [Nai mēn dipsados eidos homōsetai aien echidnē,]

Truly the form of the dipsas always resembles the viper's. The cerastes too, Gesner writes, is reckoned by many among the species of viper, evidently for the same reason. For the same Nicander describes it, verse 259:
Ἠΰτ᾽ ἔχιν· τῷ γάρ τε δομὴν ἰνδάλλεται ἴσην, [Ēyt᾽ echin; tō gar te domēn indalletai isēn,]

Like a viper; for its body appears similar to it. And in the Suda, under the word Ἔχις [Echis]: Λέγεται καὶ αἱμόῤῥους γένος ἔχεως [Legetai kai haimorrhous genos echeōs]; The haemorrhous is also said to be a kind of viper. This is [III, 137] taken from Aelian, book 15, ch. 13. Thus the hydra overcome by Hercules is called by some ἔχιδνα [echidna], that is, viper. Hence Hercules, when Achelous had been changed into a serpent, in Ovid's Metamorphoses book 9:
What fraction of the Lernaean viper will you, a single serpent, be?

So all write that the arrow with which Hercules killed Nessus was dipped in the poison of the Lernaean hydra; yet Diodorus, book 3, speaks of the same thus: Τῆς ἀκίδος τὸν ἐκ τῆς ἐχίδνης ἰὸν ἀνειληφυίας [Tēs akidos ton ek tēs echidnēs ion aneilēphuias]; Since the arrow had been imbued with the poison of the echidna (or viper). According to Homer, Iliad 2, verse 723, the Greeks left Philoctetes on the island of Lemnos
